hook.text: Ask NLTK's lemmatizer for the dictionary form of running, and you get running back.

more.text: Ran stays ran. And was comes back as wa.

noun.text: It isn't broken. Unless you say otherwise, it treats every word as a noun.

alone.text: It sees one word at a time, never the sentence.

race.text: And running really can be a noun, as in the running of the race. As a noun, it's already a dictionary form.

lookup-in.text: So what does the lookup actually do?

list.text: It takes three steps. First, each part of speech keeps a list of irregular forms.

listed.text: As a verb, ran is listed under run, and was under be. As an adjective, better is listed under good and well.

rules.text: If a word isn't listed, suffix rules make the guesses instead, like a noun's s, or a verb's ed or ing.

check.text: Last, the word and every guess are checked against WordNet, the dictionary behind the lemmatizer.

wa.text: That's where wa comes from. Was isn't on the noun list, so the s comes off, and wa is a real entry: it's short for Washington, the state.

nothing.text: Running passes as itself. But ran isn't a noun at all, so nothing survives, and you just get ran back.

tag-in.text: So where does the part of speech come from?

tagger.text: From a tagger, which reads the whole sentence. Take the runners were running and they had eaten well.

tags.text: It gives each word a Penn Treebank tag: NNS, a plural noun, for runners; VBD, a past-tense verb, for were; VBG, a verb's ing form, for running.

letter.text: WordNet knows just four parts of speech, so keep each tag's first letter.

porter.text: Porter's stemmer gets runner and run, too. But were, had and eaten pass straight through, because it only cuts endings.

close.text: So the lemmatizer was never broken. It needed the part of speech. Tag first, then lemmatize.

survive.text: Only real entries survive, and the shortest one wins.

job.text: So it can't tell what job that word is doing.

tie.text: Good and well tie at four letters, so the first one listed wins.

map.text: J, as in JJ, is an adjective, V a verb, R an adverb, and anything else, a noun.

contrast.text: Without tags, were, running, had and eaten come back unchanged. With them, were becomes be, running run, had have, and eaten eat.
